Par Coupon Yields from DNS Factors

Source: R/dns-pricing.R
dns_par_yields.Rd

Computes the par coupon yield at each maturity: the coupon rate that prices a bullet bond at par off the DNS curve.

Usage

dns_par_yields(factors, maturities, lambda = ns_lambda(3.5), frequency = 2)

Arguments

factors

Array or matrix. DNS factors, as in dns_discount_factors.

maturities

Numeric vector. Maturities in years. Each must be a whole number of coupon periods; see Details.

lambda

Numeric. DNS decay parameter lambda, per unit of maturity. Maturities here are in years, and the default places the curvature hump at 3.5 years, near the middle of a Treasury curve. It is written as ns_lambda(3.5) so the number states its own meaning; see ns_lambda. Diebold and Li's 0.0609 is a month-denominated constant and in years would place that hump at 29.4 years.

frequency

Integer. Coupon payments per year. Defaults to 2, the U.S. Treasury convention.

Value

Par yields in the same shape as dns_discount_factors, as annualised decimal rates.

Details

For a bond maturing at \(T\) with \(n = T f\) coupon dates \(t_i = i / f\), the coupon rate that makes its price equal its face value is $$c = f \, \frac{1 - P(T)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} P(t_i)}.$$ The denominator is the annuity factor: the present value of one unit paid at every coupon date.

Par yields are a coupon-bond quantity, so they are only defined on maturities that are a whole number of coupon periods. At the default semiannual frequency a 6-month maturity qualifies but a 1-month or 3-month one does not; those return NA with a warning rather than being forced onto a convention they do not have. Bill maturities belong in calculate_dns_yields or dns_discount_factors.

The gap between the par yield and the zero yield at the same maturity has two parts, which can pull in opposite directions:

  • A compounding convention term. The DNS curve is continuously compounded while the par yield is a rate payable frequency times a year, which adds roughly \(y^2 / (2f)\) and is always positive.

  • A curve shape term. Coupons are discounted at the rates earlier in the curve, not at the terminal rate alone, so an upward-sloping zero curve pulls the par yield down and an inverted one pushes it up.

The convention term dominates at short maturities, where the shape term is small; the shape term dominates further out. On a steeply upward-sloping curve the par yield is therefore slightly above the zero yield at one year and clearly below it at thirty.

See also

dns_discount_factors, dns_zero_prices

Examples

data(treasury_yields)
maturities <- as.numeric(setdiff(names(treasury_yields), "Date"))
curve <- fit_ns_model(maturities, as.numeric(treasury_yields[nrow(treasury_yields), -1]))
factors <- matrix(curve$parameters[1:3], nrow = 1)
lambda <- curve$parameters[["lambda"]]

coupon_maturities <- c(0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 30)
zero <- calculate_dns_yields(factors, coupon_maturities, lambda)
par <- dns_par_yields(factors, coupon_maturities, lambda)

data.frame(
  maturity = coupon_maturities,
  zero_pct = round(zero[1, ] * 100, 3),
  par_pct = round(par[1, ] * 100, 3)
)
#>   maturity zero_pct par_pct
#> 1      0.5    4.282   4.328
#> 2      1.0    4.216   4.261
#> 3      2.0    4.196   4.240
#> 4      5.0    4.386   4.423
#> 5     10.0    4.621   4.639
#> 6     30.0    4.824   4.812
